sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area/Volume
sections.content: Briefly define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the signed area of a parallelogram formed by two vectors (column vectors). Remind students that the absolute value equals the area, and the sign indicates orientation.
sections.example: Visualize a unit square being transformed by vectors v1=[2, 0] and v2=[0, 2]; the area becomes 4, which is exactly the determinant of the matrix [2, 0; 0, 2].

sections.title: Framing the System as Vector Scaling
sections.content: Represent a linear system Ax = b as x * a1 + y * a2 = b. Geometrically, this means we are finding the weights (x and y) required to scale vectors a1 and a2 to reach the target point b.
sections.example: Imagine a robot arm (the origin) trying to reach a 'treat' at point b. Vector a1 points to a cherry, a2 points to a berry. x and y are the quantities needed to reach b.

sections.title: Cramer's Rule: The Geometric Swap
sections.content: Explain that replacing a column of A with b creates a new parallelogram. For x, we look at the area formed by b and a2. The ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original determinant A gives the value of x.
sections.example: Show an animation where the vector a1 is 'pushed out' and replaced by b. The 'shadow' area formed by b and a2, divided by the area of a1 and a2, precisely yields the scaling factor x.

sections.title: Visual Synthesis & Application
sections.content: Summarize how this generalizes to higher dimensions (volumes). Emphasize that when the determinant is zero, the vectors are collinear (flat), meaning the 'volume' is zero, confirming why Cramer’s Rule fails for singular matrices.
sections.example: A 3D example: Three squirrels moving along vectors v1, v2, v3. If the vectors are coplanar, the 'volume' is zero, and they cannot reach any arbitrary point b in 3D space, demonstrating the geometric constraint of the system.
